title: A Note towards the Understanding of Lighting Quality

findings.antecedent: regular arrays of recessed luminaires (common in offices)
findings.mechanism: lack of visual variety in a windowless environment (speculative)
findings.quote: the regular arrays of recessed luminaires, the most common way of lighting offices, are the least preferred.

findings.antecedent: prismatic 'batwing' luminaires (a type of recessed luminaire)
findings.quote: the prismatic 'batwing' which was rated very low

findings.antecedent: complexity and brightness of lighting design
findings.mechanism: both factors must operate together for increased attractiveness
findings.source: Page 2 summary, Page 10 discussion, Page 11 discussion
findings.quote: Complexity and brightness together: perhaps that is what people want in the lighting of their offices.

findings.mechanism: high stress value (23.5%) indicated uninformative results, possibly due to sequential presentation of random mock-ups
findings.quote: The results of the analysis were inconclusive... stress value was 23.5 percent... the procedure is in this case uninformative.

findings.consequent: factors explaining variance in lighting appraisals
findings.mechanism: two underlying factors identified from subjective ratings
findings.quote: It was found that only two factors were necessary in which 79 percent of the variance was accounted for.

findings.antecedent: semantic differential scales implying degrees of subjective brightness (e.g., Frugal-Lavish, Dim-Bright)
findings.mechanism: scales with high loadings define Factor I as subjective brightness
findings.quote: high loadings on Factor I occur with scales implying degrees of subjective brightness

findings.antecedent: semantic differential scales implying degrees of interest (e.g., Mysterious-Obvious, Uninteresting-Interesting, Simple-Complex)
findings.mechanism: scales with high loadings define Factor II as subjective interest/complexity
findings.quote: high loadings on Factor II occur with scales implying degrees of interest.

findings.mechanism: Log cylindrical illuminance is a good predictor of subjective brightness

findings.antecedent: Log Cylindrical Illuminance (physical measure, excluding situation K)
findings.consequent: Brightness factor scores (subjective measure, excluding situation K)
findings.mechanism: Log cylindrical illuminance is a good predictor of subjective brightness, with improved correlation when outlier K is removed
Log vertical illuminance is a good predictor of subjective brightness

findings.antecedent: Log Vertical Illuminance (physical measure, excluding situation K)
findings.consequent: Brightness factor scores (subjective measure, excluding situation K)
findings.mechanism: Log vertical illuminance is a good predictor of subjective brightness, with improved correlation when outlier K is removed

findings.antecedent: lighting situations using diffuse sources only (wall-lighting or recessed)
findings.mechanism: lack of distinct boundaries or variation in luminance
findings.quote: All eight situations using diffuse sources only... are placed towards the uninteresting side of the neutral on this factor

findings.antecedent: lighting situations with one or more focused sources
findings.mechanism: more boundaries separating areas of light and shade in a relatively sharp contour; wide range in luminances with more than one peak
findings.quote: all 10 situations with one or more focused sources are towards the interesting side of neutral.

findings.antecedent: lighting situations that are brighter and more complex (higher Factor I and Factor II scores)
findings.mechanism: brightness and complexity factors must operate together for increased attractiveness
findings.quote: the brighter more complex situations being the highest point on the contour map (lightest shading). It should be noted that making a simple situation brighter does not make it better, and neither does making a dim situation more complex; both factors must operate together.

findings.antecedent: situations using only one type of luminaire
findings.quote: situations using only one type of luminaire occur lower down on the slopes

findings.antecedent: smaller source luminaires with more directional quality
findings.mechanism: these luminaires contribute to complexity and distinct boundaries, leading to higher preference
findings.quote: the smaller source luminaires, with more directional quality, are concentrated towards the preference peak.

findings.mechanism: efficient sources often correspond to diffuse, less complex lighting, which is less preferred
findings.quote: efficient fluorescent sources low on the preference slopes

findings.mechanism: inefficient sources often correspond to focused, more complex lighting, which is more preferred
findings.quote: inefficient concentrated tungsten sources towards the peak

findings.mechanism: comparable but not identical, due to dimmers equalizing desk-top illuminance across different sources
findings.quote: iso-consumption contours are comparable with the iso-preference ones. Though they are comparable they are not identical

stimuli.description: An office mock-up (10 ft by 15 ft and 8 ft high, windowless) furnished as a two-person office, with 18 different lighting situations created by manipulating six types of luminaires (ceiling recessed, wall lighting, down-lights, desk lights, track lights) and their dimming levels/control panels.
stimuli.source: Experimental design and procedure section, Table 2.1, Figure 2.1, 2.2, 2.3

tables.description: Lists the 18 lighting situations and the luminaires used for each.
Shows the Latin-square design for the orders of presentation of lighting situations to subjects.

Lists physical measures for each of the 18 lighting situations, including horizontal, vertical, scalar, vector, cylindrical illuminance, vector/scalar ratio, ESI, vertical illuminance (+50°), and total energy consumption in watts.
Shows factor loadings for 13 semantic differential scales on Factor I (Brightness) and Factor II (Interest).
Lists Factor I (Brightness) scores, Factor II (Interest) scores, and Preference Rating for each of the 18 lighting situations.
Lists Pearson correlation coefficients (r) between Brightness factor scores and various illuminance measures for 18 and 17 situations (K omitted).

limitations: MDSCAL analysis was inconclusive with a stress value of 23.5 percent, indicating considerable unhandled information, possibly due to random mock-ups presented sequentially rather than simultaneously.
The study could not empirically determine if the preference for brighter and more complex lighting continues to extreme values or if it curtails beyond a certain limit.
The windowless environment might have exaggerated the low ratings of situations due to a lack of visual variety.
The experimental procedure, which did not allow subjects to work for a long time in the same environment, might have made variety more desirable.
